name: YOUR CRESS IS ON MY LIST BURGER (comes with watercress)

recipe.history:
Watercress (Nasturtium officinale) is among the oldest leafy vegetables consumed by humans, with fossil records and historical evidence placing its consumption in the diet of Persian soldiers as early as 400 BCE, where Xenophon records that cress was fed to Persian youth alongside bread to build strength and vigor. The plant is native to Europe and Asia and grows as a semi-aquatic perennial in clear, cold, running water — stream beds, freshwater springs, and irrigation channels — with the water's flow providing constant aeration and nutrition that produces the plant's characteristic peppery, mustard-hot, slightly bitter flavor profile. The spicy compounds in watercress, principally phenethyl isothiocyanate (PEITC), are the same family of compounds found in horseradish, wasabi, and mustard greens, and are produced when the plant is chewed and its cells are ruptured, releasing the enzyme myrosinase to act on glucosinolate precursors. In Victorian England watercress was called the 'poor man's bread' — it was sold in the streets of London for a halfpenny a bunch and eaten as a breakfast food by workers who could afford no bread, a piece of social history that gives the plant a dignity rooted not in luxury but in survival.

Watercress came to prominence in American culinary culture through two distinct routes. The first was the fine-dining route, where watercress appeared as a classic French and English-style salad green on white-tablecloth menus throughout the mid-twentieth century, typically in combination with endive, poached egg, or a sharp vinaigrette. The second was the health-food route of the 1970s and 1980s, when nutritionists began publicizing watercress's exceptional nutritional profile — it is one of the most nutrient-dense plants measurable by the CDC's power foods scoring system, ranking first among all vegetables in some analyses. On a burger, watercress functions as an upgrade to lettuce in every measurable way: it provides a peppery heat that acts as a condiment, a structural crispness that holds up better than iceberg against a hot patty, and a visual elegance — the small round leaves, the slender stems, the deep green color — that signals to the eater that something has been thought about here.

I developed a deep appreciation for watercress through a period of obsessive salad-making during which I was trying to understand what made certain bitter and peppery greens more interesting than their mild counterparts. Watercress rewarded that attention more than anything else I tested. Raw and fresh it is sharp and bracing; wilted slightly by heat it softens into something almost creamy, the bitterness mellowing into a green savor. I discovered by accident the pairing of watercress with a beef burger when I was making a quick dinner with whatever was in the refrigerator and grabbed the watercress bunch I'd bought for a salad. The peppery hit of the cress against the fatty richness of the medium-rare beef was instant and obvious, the way some flavor combinations are — the kind that make you feel briefly that you have discovered something universal rather than invented something personal. The lemon-shallot dressing I now toss the cress in before it goes on the burger is essential; the acid brightens the pepper notes and adds a dimension that plain undressed watercress alone misses.

Watercress belongs on a medium-rare burger because the conversation between pepper and fat only happens when the fat is present and accessible. A medium-rare patty at 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit has rendered fat that is warm and fluid, present in every bite, and when the peppery isothiocyanates of fresh watercress hit that fat they diffuse into it and become part of the overall flavor of the burger rather than sitting on top of it as a separate element. This is the chemistry of fat-soluble flavor compounds, and it is the reason that peppery greens taste better on medium-rare beef than on any other temperature. Beyond that, the warmth of the rested patty wilts the watercress just slightly — two or three degrees of passive wilting — which releases a small amount of cell liquid from the cress that mingles with the beef juices in the bun. This is not a recipe for the impatient or the careless. Cook to 130 to 135. Rest. Dress the cress. Assemble and eat.
ingredients: 1 large shallot, very thinly sliced into rings
Fine sea salt and freshly cracked black pepper
30g watercress leaves, blanched 30 seconds, squeezed dry, finely chopped
1 tbsp fresh flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped
Fine sea salt and white pepper
instructions: 1. Make the English muffin-style buns: Combine flour, yeast, sugar, and salt in a stand mixer bowl. Add warm milk, egg, butter, and white wine vinegar. Mix on low then knead on medium for 8 minutes until smooth.

2. Cover and let rise 1.5 hours until doubled. Divide into 4 portions and shape into thick discs about 1 inch tall. Dust both sides generously with semolina flour. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Proof covered 45 minutes.

3. Heat a dry griddle or large skillet over medium-low heat. Cook the buns for 7 to 8 minutes per side until cooked through and the semolina crust is golden. (These cook like traditional English muffins on a griddle, no oven required.) Cool on a rack. They will have a characteristic nooks-and-crannies interior when split with a fork.

4. Make the watercress compound butter: Combine softened butter, chopped blanched watercress, grated garlic, lemon zest, lemon juice, salt, and white pepper. Beat until fully combined. Roll into a log in plastic wrap and refrigerate until firm.

5. Make the lemon-herb aioli: Whisk egg yolks, garlic, and Dijon together in a bowl. Whisking constantly, add olive oil in a very thin stream until a thick emulsion forms. Whisk in lemon juice and zest. Fold in parsley and chives. Season with salt and white pepper. Refrigerate until needed.

6. Dress the watercress: Whisk together olive oil, lemon juice, Dijon, and honey in a small bowl. Season with salt and pepper. Toss watercress and sliced shallot with just enough dressing to coat lightly — do this no more than 5 minutes before serving to prevent wilting.

7. Prepare patties: Divide ground beef into 4 portions (about 170g). Shape into 3/4-inch-thick patties. Add a few drops of Worcestershire sauce to each patty face before seasoning with kosher salt and black pepper. Let rest 5 minutes before cooking.
8. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Cook patties 3 minutes first side undisturbed.
9. Flip, immediately add aged white cheddar to each patty. Tent with a dome. Cook 90 seconds to 2 minutes more.
10. Check internal temperature — pull at 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Rest on a rack for 3 minutes.

11. While patties rest, split the English muffin buns (use a fork to split if desired, for proper nooks and crannies). Spread watercress compound butter on both cut faces. Toast cut-side down in the pan over medium heat for 60 to 90 seconds.
12. Assemble: Spread lemon-herb aioli on the bottom bun over the melted compound butter. Add sliced avocado fanned out across the bottom, season with flaky salt.
13. Place the rested cheese-topped patty on top. Mound a generous handful of dressed watercress and shallot over the patty.
14. Add 4 radish slices over the watercress for extra crunch and color. Spread a small amount of aioli on the top bun, close the burger, and serve immediately.
